clue.text: A little boy in blue maybe turning round

indicators.note: something turning faces the other way, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: a policeman, the 'boy in blue' of slang, is a cop
a round shape looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A small boy dressed in blue spins round and round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A little boy' reads as one phrase, but 'A little' is the definition and 'boy in blue' is the policeman.
explanation.definitionFit: Poco is the Italian musical direction meaning slightly or somewhat, as in poco a poco.

clue.text: What wannabe fiancé may do in jeweller's around East Yorks town

indicators.note: to sit around something is to surround it, so one piece is placed outside another

parts.words: What wannabe fiancé may do in jeweller's
parts.note: a would-be groom shopping for the engagement must choose a band for the finger
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A nervous man about to propose browses a jeweller's shop in a Yorkshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: The proposer will PICK RING, and E for East goes into the middle of that phrase. 'East Yorks' looks like a region, but East belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Pickering is a market town in North Yorkshire, on the edge of the North York Moors.

clue.text: Royal Academy's head works in C&A

indicators.note: placing one thing in another means it goes between the outer pieces

parts.note: C and A taken as written, the name of the high-street clothing chain

indicators.note: the head of a word is its front, so only its opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of Academy
a mill is a works, a factory

explanation.surface: The head of the Royal Academy has some piece of art on show in a C&A clothing store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Royal Academy' reads as one institution, but 'Royal' is the definition. C&A was a British and European high-street clothing chain.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen Camilla, wife of King Charles III, is a member of the British royal family.

clue.text: Cher ousts Queen with some current number one

indicators.note: to oust someone is to throw them out, so letters are removed

parts.note: the singer's name taken as written
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword Queen
an amp is a measured quantity of electric current

explanation.surface: The pop star Cher knocks a Queen song off the top spot with her latest chart number one.
explanation.walkthrough: Cher, Queen, current and number one all suggest the pop charts; 'current' is electricity, not 'present-day'.
explanation.definitionFit: A champ, short for champion, is the winner, the one ranked first in a competition.

clue.text: Lake view overlooked by person inside

indicators.note: in a down clue what is overlooked sits below what looks down on it, fixing the order

parts.note: a con, short for convict, is a person inside prison
a stance is a view or opinion

explanation.surface: A lake view seen from a prisoner's cell window.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside' is slang for in prison. 'View' sounds like scenery but is an opinion.
explanation.definitionFit: Lake Constance is the large Alpine lake bordered by Germany, Austria and Switzerland.

clue.text: Help when reading news report of traffic jam?

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the sound of the words counts rather than the spelling

parts.note: a traffic jam is a queue of cars, or autos

explanation.surface: A newsreader needs help with a traffic bulletin about a jam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'News report' looks like one phrase, but 'news' ends the definition and 'report of' signals the sound. Autocue is a British trade name for a teleprompter.
explanation.definitionFit: An Autocue scrolls a script in front of the camera lens so a presenter can read the bulletin while looking at viewers.

clue.text: Backing way of working in advertising

parts.note: to be pro something is to back it
MO, modus operandi, is a way of working

explanation.surface: Someone supports a particular style of working in the advertising business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' sounds like support for a method, but it is a word of its own. The definition is a noun used loosely as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A promo is a promotional piece, a short advert or trailer used to publicise something.

clue.text: Irrational and illogical, throwing away a book

indicators.note: what is thrown away is discarded, so those letters drop out

parts.note: something illogical is absurd
a as written, with B the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: Someone acts unreasonably, tossing aside a book in a fit of pique.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irrational' reads as a mood, but it is the mathematical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: In mathematics a surd is an irrational root such as the square root of two, so the noun names an irrational quantity.

clue.text: Rating chocolate bar she unwrapped: it's very soggy

parts.note: a rating is an ordinary sailor, and an old salt is a sailor
Mars is a well-known chocolate bar

indicators.note: unwrapping takes off the outer layer, so only the inside letter is kept

parts.note: the inner letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone scores a chocolate bar after unwrapping it, finding it horribly soggy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rating' looks like a score, but it is the naval term for a sailor below officer rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A salt marsh is coastal land regularly flooded by the tide, so the ground is waterlogged and boggy.

clue.text: Crazy vocalist follows cover of Roxette in lounge

indicators.note: what follows comes after, which fixes the order of the two pieces
a cover is the outside, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the band's name
Patsy Cline was the singer famous for the song Crazy

explanation.surface: A mad singer performs a Roxette cover song in a hotel lounge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crazy' looks like an insult, but it is the title of Patsy Cline's best-known song; 'cover' is not a cover version.
explanation.definitionFit: To lounge is to lie back lazily, which is what one does when one reclines on a sofa.

clue.text: I state cutting smooth hair is a key alternative?

indicators.note: something cutting into another splits it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: to comb hair is to smooth it
taken as written
a state is a nation
a lock is a tress of hair

explanation.surface: Someone declares that cutting hair smooth is the key alternative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting' tells you the state and its pronoun split the smooth-hair pair in two. The question mark flags a definition by description rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A combination lock opens with a sequence of numbers rather than a physical key, so it replaces one.

clue.text: Join forces with paragon of virtue on line, oddly

indicators.note: in an across clue placing one thing on another puts it after, fixing the order
done oddly means done in a strange way, so the letters come out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
a saint is a paragon of virtue, abbreviated ST

explanation.surface: Someone teams up with a model of goodness online, which seems odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On line' looks like the word online, but it splits: 'on' places the saint after, and 'line' is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To enlist is to sign up for the armed forces, so to join the forces in the military sense.

clue.text: Eccentric who fried mince cakes in dish

indicators.note: to cake something in is to encase it in a crust, so one piece wraps another
something eccentric is off-centre and odd, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: frying reduces food to a changed state, so these letters are mixed up too

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: An oddball who fries minced meat bakes it into a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: Two separate anagrams: the scrambled pronoun sits inside the scrambled meat. 'Cakes' is a verb meaning encrusts.
explanation.definitionFit: Chow mein is a Chinese-style plate of stir-fried noodles with meat and vegetables.

clue.text: Speaker's artlessness viewed from a certain perspective

indicators.note: what a speaker produces is heard, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

parts.note: artlessness is naive simplicity, innocence

explanation.surface: A lecturer's naivety looks different depending on your point of view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speaker's' looks possessive, but it only tells you to listen.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is used to qualify a statement as true only partly or in one particular way of looking at it.

clue.text: Revolver in place, loaded by a famous marksman

indicators.note: something loaded is filled from inside, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: a site is a place
a as written, plus William Tell, who shot an apple off his son's head

explanation.surface: A gun stored somewhere is loaded by a well-known sharpshooter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolver' and 'marksman' paint a pistol, but the revolver here goes round a planet.
explanation.definitionFit: A satellite orbits, or revolves around, a planet, so it is something that revolves.

clue.text: Perhaps setter is one bringing in the punters

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a dog, of which a setter is one example
second meaning: a tout who calls out to passers-by outside a fairground show

explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' tempts the solver to think of the puzzle's compiler, but it is the gun dog. Punters are paying customers.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog that barks is jokingly a barker, and a fairground crier who shouts to draw customers in is also so called.

clue.text: See red garment clothing skinny person out of India

indicators.note: to clothe something is to wrap it, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: a blouse is a garment

indicators.note: something taken out of a group is removed, so that letter drops away

parts.note: a waif is a thin, frail person
India is I in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone is furious that a red dress is draped on a thin model from India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red garment' looks like one phrase, but 'red' belongs to the definition; 'out of India' removes the letter for India rather than giving an origin.
explanation.definitionFit: To see red and to blow a fuse are both idioms for suddenly losing one's temper.

clue.text: Prat breaks collars again

parts.note: prat is old slang for the buttocks, the rear
breaks are rests

explanation.surface: A fool snaps his shirt collars once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prat' means an idiot in British slang, but its older sense is the backside.
explanation.definitionFit: To collar someone is slang for arresting them, so collaring again is arresting a second time.

clue.text: A place to drive introduced by travel feature

indicators.note: what introduces something comes before it, which fixes the order

parts.note: to go is to travel
taken as written
a golfer drives off from the tee

explanation.surface: A travel magazine article highlights a good place to go driving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' suggests a car, but it is a golf stroke; 'feature' sounds like a newspaper piece, but it is a facial feature.
explanation.definitionFit: A goatee is a small pointed beard on the chin, a distinctive part of someone's face.

clue.text: A loser's het up, ill-equipped for a row

indicators.note: someone het up is agitated and stirred, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A sore loser gets worked up and is in no state for an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' rhymes with cow in the surface, an argument, but the answer needs the boating sense. 'Het up' is British for agitated.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat without oars cannot be propelled by rowing, so its crew is poorly equipped for it.

clue.text: Overexcited reaction from relative texting you "LOL!"

parts.note: bro is short for brother, a relative
in text-speak 'you' is written U
LOL, laugh out loud, is the texted laugh

explanation.surface: A family member overreacts by sending a laughing text message.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Texting' tells you to write 'you' as a text message would.
explanation.definitionFit: A brouhaha is a noisy fuss or commotion, an excited overreaction to something.

clue.text: In Bologna on vacation, dry gin gets drunk

indicators.note: a place on vacation is emptied of its people, so only the outer letters remain

parts.note: the first and last letters of the city's name

indicators.note: getting drunk leaves one in a muddle, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: TT, teetotal, means not drinking alcohol
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: On holiday in Bologna, a teetotaller nonetheless gets drunk on gin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a preposition leading the surface, but it is the definition, a cricket term.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket the side that is in is the one currently at the crease, taking its innings.

clue.text: One might run articles without hindrance

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: the indefinite and definite articles
a let is an obstruction, as in 'without let or hindrance'

explanation.surface: Someone could publish news stories freely, without being obstructed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without hindrance' reads as 'freely', but 'without' means outside, and 'run articles' is a sprinter rather than a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Track athletes are competitors who race, so a sprinter or distance runner is a typical example.

clue.text: Land embracing papal illumination

indicators.note: to embrace is to hug, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: to alight is to land, as a bird or passenger does
RC, Roman Catholic, describes what belongs to the Pope's church

explanation.surface: A country receives a divine revelation from the Pope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Land' looks like a noun, a country, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An arc-light produces brilliant light from an electric spark between electrodes, used for floodlighting.

clue.text: Good means of viewing Highland features?

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
a lens is used to see through

explanation.surface: A tourist wonders what device is best for viewing the Scottish landscape.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as an example: the Highlands of Scotland are full of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A glen is a narrow valley, a typical landscape element of the Scottish mountains.

clue.text: Hurrah! Seat arranged in stadium

definitions.note: the answer is the person after whom the stadium is named

indicators.note: letters that are arranged are set out in a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A spectator cheers as their seat is allocated in the arena.
explanation.walkthrough: The tennis champion gives his name to the arena, so the definition is the stadium's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ashe Stadium in New York is the main court of the US Open tennis tournament.

clue.text: Half of Bordeaux and crisps on the house is what you may get in bars

definitions.text: what you may get in bars

indicators.note: in an across clue placing something on another puts it after, fixing the order

parts.note: demi is French for half
a semi is a semi-detached house, the usual British suburban home
Quavers are a British brand of cheese-flavoured crisps

explanation.surface: Half a bottle of Bordeaux and free crisps is the kind of thing a pub offers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the house' means free in the surface, but here it places the crisps after the house. 'Bars' are pubs in the surface but musical bars in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A demisemiquaver is a thirty-second note, one of the short notes that fill a bar of music.

clue.text: See 21
Sudanese guerrilla lines move smoothly

indicators.note: a lining sits inside something, so the answer is found within the words

parts.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A Sudanese rebel force advances in smooth formation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines' looks like rows of fighters, but it is a verb: the words line the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To segue is to make a seamless transition from one thing to the next, as in music or conversation.

clue.text: Visits Oxford and Durham, perhaps

definitions.meaning: first meaning: calls on, as in going to see a friend
second meaning: bishops' dioceses, of which these two cities are examples

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a tour of university towns, but the cities are examples of bishoprics.
explanation.definitionFit: To call on someone is to go and see them, and a bishop's seat of authority is his see.
